# ============================================================================
# ERN policy-evidence page — the four P&#39;s, and the floor under them.
# Edit the copy here, then rebuild:
#
#     quarto render policy.qmd
#
# That overwrites policy.html in place. git is the safety net — review
# `git diff policy.html` before committing.
#
# The page chrome lives in _extensions/ern/policy/template.html. Everything a
# person normally wants to change (headings, the framework tiles, every
# plank, the legend, the callout, links, footer) is a field below, so the
# template should rarely need touching.
#
# NOTE: values here are parsed as Markdown. Write &#39; for a straight
# apostrophe, which is what the rest of the site uses. Do not backslash-escape:
# inside a folded block scalar (>-) YAML keeps the backslash and it lands on
# the page. Colons and URLs need no escaping.
#
# AUGUST 2026 MERGE: this page now carries the plank cards from ERN&#39;s
# draft national housing rights charter (library/quarto/housing-rights-charter
# in the evictionresearch repo). The four P sections keep this page&#39;s
# claim headlines; the planks inside use the charter&#39;s card format — a
# tier pill (T1 fastest/largest effect, T3 structural/slow), an Evidence or
# Reasoned badge, and a national-status mark (&#10003; federal law /
# &#9681; some states / &#8856; ran nationally, ended / &#9675; nowhere yet).
# A fifth section, The floor, carries the charter&#39;s Article V.
#
# FACT DISCIPLINE: every plank marked Evidence was checked against its named
# source. The charter&#39;s planks were verified by source-fetching agents on
# 2026-08-27; the full merged page was re-verified claim by claim on
# 2026-08-28 (verification ledger at the end of this comment). Planks marked
# Reasoned are argued from mechanism or arithmetic and labeled as such. Do
# not add a number without doing the same.
#
# DO NOT CLAIM (carried from the charter&#39;s verification):
#   - No one-to-one prevention-cost vs homelessness-cost ledger; magnitudes
#     only (the populations differ — the Evans card says so on the page).
#   - Evans 2016 is a funding-availability quasi-experiment, not an RCT.
#     The paper&#39;s own body ties the 76% to a six-month horizon (88% at
#     three months), so "within six months" is correct — a 2026-08-28
#     full-text read reversed the earlier abstract-only lock.
#   - Humphries NBER 33155: $1,252 is the AVERAGE rent owed by move-out,
#     not a median at filing. The verified filing-month figure is "90% of
#     evicted tenants owe at least one month of rent."
#   - Auckland figure is 23% (Economic Inquiry 2026), not 20–35%.
#   - Mast 2023 moves 45–70 PEOPLE, not units.
#   - NYC right-to-counsel: cite FY2023&#39;s 84%; FY2024&#39;s 89% uses a
#     broadened definition.
#   - Mortality 19%/40% is Graetz et al., Soc Sci & Medicine 2024 — not the
#     JAMA COVID paper.
#   - Do not say "rent control chills construction" against capped-increase
#     designs that exempt new construction; Diamond et al. found conversion,
#     not suppressed building.
#   - Old research-page claims that failed checking stay dropped: the "NYC
#     evictions fell 41%" figure, the "first statewide just-cause" credit to
#     Oregon (New Jersey, 1974), a Michigan 87% figure.
#   - "Maryland filings fell by more than half" after the 10-day notice:
#     no source found (2026-08-28 search); dropped.
#   - NYC borough range 72&ndash;93% is FY2024, whose "remain in home" metric
#     is the broadened one; kept off with the FY24 89%.
#   - Benfer&#39;s $1B&#8594;$4.5B figure is the broader business+landlord
#     background-check industry, confirmed only via a reproduced abstract;
#     kept off. Same for "nine in ten landlords screen" (a TransUnion
#     survey via CFPB fn 14; CFPB&#39;s own text is more cautious).
#   - Do not write "SOI laws roughly halve denial rates" — the HUD study
#     disclaims evaluating the laws; Philadelphia (67% denial) had one.
#   - (2026-10-08) Humphries $1,252 is the average balance at move-out for
#     ALL tenants in the sample; evicted tenants owed about $3,229 (3.5
#     months). Never present $1,252 as what evicted tenants owed.
#   - (2026-10-08) Reinvestment Fund: 7.4% (all assisted, 6 months) vs
#     42.2% (unassisted); 4.2% is the mediated-agreement subgroup (n=119);
#     33.3% at 21 months is all assisted cases. Do not pair 4.2% with 33.3%.
#   - (2026-10-08) CCP 1161.2 unmasks a record 60 days after filing only
#     when the plaintiff won within 60 days; later wins need a court order.
#   - (2026-10-08) Covenant Homeownership: no official page states a
#     $150,000 cap; do not print one. HUD opened a Fair Housing Act
#     investigation March 24, 2026 (letter to WSHFC), unresolved.
#   - (2026-10-08) RCW 59.20.370 states no notice period; three months'
#     notice is RCW 59.20.090(2). RCW 59.20.325's 70 days is to form a
#     tenant organization and declare interest, not to bid.
#   - (2026-10-08) Stout Cleveland does not say the prevention rate fell;
#     cumulative 83% vs 76% for 2025 cases; overall goal achievement fell
#     80% to 75%, driven by the rent-assistance goal.
#
# VERIFICATION LEDGER (2026-08-28, six source-fetching agents; quote +
# location recorded for every item; agent transcripts in the session tasks
# directory). V = verified at source; P = verified via mirror/snippet
# because the primary was bot-blocked.
#   Humphries NBER 33155 p.10-11 (90% >=1 month V; $1,252 = avg owed by
#     move-out V); ERN/Penn HUD ERA eval via evictionresearch.net/hud-era
#     (53%/65% LA, 45%/673k, 700+ counties/22 states, proxy-rules lesson V;
#     "45% lower odds forced move" FAILED -> replaced with 1/3-vs-18%
#     informal-eviction stat); Treasury 10.8M/$46.55B V; Eviction Lab
#     50.3%/1.36M/3M+ V; Minn. Stat. 462A.204 (1993) V; Reinvestment Fund
#     pp.6-11 (4.2/42.2/33.3) V; WA ERPP 78% p.29, sunset 6/30/2023 V;
#     Phila. 9-811 eff. 1/1/2022 P (30/45-day nuance -> day-count dropped;
#     2026-10-08: Bill 240245 (2024) removed the sunset, 30-day minimum);
#     TDHCA 25k+/$243M V; Evans Science pp.694-698 (76% IS the 6-month
#     figure; quasi-experiment) V; LEO Santa Clara $2.47/$1 V; NAEH
#     $35,578 V; HUD AHAR 745,652 V; NASEM PSH highlights p.2 V; Family
#     Options p.36 and p.xxxiii (homelessness more than halved; the p.45
#     cite recorded in August was wrong, corrected 2026-10-08) V.
#   NCCRC 28 jurisdictions + 4%/84% (~43-study compilation) V; RCW
#     59.18.640 (2021; "first state" via ABA Journal) V; NYC OCJ FY2023
#     p.10 84% V; Furman pp.2,6 (54%, 40%; 64 OCA jurisdictions) V; Stout
#     Philly $12.74 (Phila. Bar page) V; Stout Cleveland pp.6-10
#     (83/70, ~50% no defense, back-rent quote, assistance wind-down) V;
#     MD FY2017 abstract Table DC-2 144,058 landlord-tenant filed V;
#     Losing Home 4,788 (2017, King County) P - report PDF currently 404s;
#     Md. Ch. 746 10-day notice eff. 10/1/2021 V; SB 5600 14-day + RCW
#     59.18.410 redemption V; NPHL fact sheet pp.1,3 (1-in-3 2014 = Leung
#     et al.; $76/3.11 = Gomory et al. HPD 2023) V.
#   Porton 22% (abstract wording) P; So HPD 2023 P (journal 403, full PDF
#     mirror read); CFPB 16,000+ V; Hepburn 19.9/32.7 p.653 V; FCRA 15 USC

#     (7%+CPI max 10%), .710 (12-yr exemption), 59.20.370 (5% lots),

#   JCHS 2026 pp.3,15,25 (9.3M/2.5M/30%; 22.7M ~49%) + p.2,21 (547k->416k
#     multifamily STARTS) V; PAHRC pp.5-6 (5M/10%; 374,497) V; CARB
#     pp.5,9,12,13,56 (ratings; 3/4 unsubsidized; CLT "economic
#     resources"; Gallaher 58% = completed TOPA process and could afford

#     (70-day window, opportunity to compete; CLTs in 59.20.030(4)) V;
#     PL 119-101 sec.1001 (350 homes, no divestment, 7/11/2026) V;
#     Raymond et al. Atlanta Fed CED 04-16 pp.1,17 (8% more likely to
#     file) V; Colburn UC Press V.
#   Asquith REStat 5-7% V; Auckland 23% + 3/4 upzoned (EI 2026) V; JUE
#     2023 construction V; Pew Minneapolis 12/1 vs 4/14 P (Pew bot-blocks;
#     MN Senate PDF capture); Mast 45-70 people, most within 3 years P
#     (RePEc abstract); Seattle Prop 1A 5%/$53M V; RCW 39.33.015 V;
#     Covenant $150k/0%/$75-100M (WSHFC FAQ p.3) V; 3SHB 1491 50-year
#     affordability V.
#   GAO-24-106637 (2/28/2024) quote V; Gromis PNAS 3.6M/~7%/99.9M/1M
#     (PMC copy) V; Cityscape 5.5:1 p.281 V; SB 1160: Senate 39-0
#     5/27/2026, out of Approps 8/13, on Assembly floor as of 8/28 V;
#     CBPP 5.1M + 3-in-4 P (bot-blocked, snippet-confirmed); Collinson
#     QJE (3.4pp/300%, -14% yr2, +29% hospital visits, female and Black
#     tenants) V; CMTO 15->53 (full services bundle) V; Graetz SSM 2024
#     19/40 V; Himmelstein JAMA Peds V; NLIHC Gap 2026 pp.4-17
#     (7.2M/11M/35/74%) V.
#   ERN-internal, repo provenance: HPRM top-5-of-184 process clocks
#     (understanding-eviction.html, verified July 2026); six states
#     publish case-level data + Smith v. Wasatch (law/02_evidence_base.md).
#   2026-09-14 companion-database pass (reference shelf + plank pointers):
#     NLIHC State and Local Tenant Protections Database
#     (nlihc.org/tenant-protections): tracks RTC, source of income, record
#     sealing, anti-rent-gouging, just cause across states, territories,

#     Database (with Temple Beasley&#39;s Center for Public Health Law

#     Housing Solutions Lab policy library

#   2026-10-08 RE-VERIFICATION (four source-fetching agents, every claim

#     681 (GovBuddy action list, Governor's 9/27 update); DOJ v. RealPage

title: "What keeps people housed — Eviction Research Network"

meta:
  canonical: "https://evictionresearch.net/policy.html"
  author: "Eviction Research Network, UC Berkeley"
  og_title: "What keeps people housed — Eviction Research Network"
  og_image: "https://evictionresearch.net/images/ern_logo/1Av2/EvictionStudy_logo_v09_1A_LOGO_BANNER.png"
  description: >-
    The four P&#39;s of eviction policy — prevent, protect, preserve,
    produce — as thirty policy planks with the measured evidence behind
    each, plus the data, funding, and organizing floor they all stand on.
    Written for legislators and the staff who draft the bills.
  short_description: >-
    Four kinds of policy with measured effects on eviction — prevent,
    protect, preserve, produce — as thirty planks, each marked evidence
    or reasoned.
  keywords: >-
    eviction prevention policy, four Ps housing, housing rights charter,
    right to counsel, eviction diversion, emergency rental assistance, just
    cause eviction, eviction record sealing, source of income
    discrimination, housing preservation, housing supply, social housing,
    eviction data, Eviction Research Network

  logo: "images/ern_logo/1Av2/EvictionStudy_logo_v09_1A_LOGO_BANNER.png"

  logo_stacked_reversed: "images/ern_logo/1A/EvictionStudy_logo_v09_1A_LOGO_STACK_REV.png"

hero:
  eyebrow: "Policy evidence"
  h1_lead: "What keeps people"
  h1_em: "housed."
  lede: >-
    Eviction responds to policy. This page sorts the interventions with
    measured effects into four kinds, the four P&#39;s, ordered from
    fastest-acting to slowest. For each one it says what it does, what the
    evidence shows, and where it stands. A fifth section names the floor every lever stands
    on. Written for legislators and the staff who draft the bills.
  meta: >-
    **Four P&#39;s · Thirty planks** · Each marked Evidence or Reasoned ·
    Every statistic carries its source · Updated October 2026
  jump:
    - label: "01 · Prevent"
      href: "#prevent"
    - label: "02 · Protect"
      href: "#protect"
    - label: "03 · Preserve"
      href: "#preserve"
    - label: "04 · Produce"
      href: "#produce"
    - label: "05 · The floor"
      href: "#floor"

stats:
  - v: "3.6"
    unit: "million"
    l: >-
      Eviction cases landlords file in an average year. Almost 7% of renting
      households face one.
    s: >-
      <a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2116169119">Gromis et
      al., PNAS 2022</a>
  - v: "5.5"
    unit: "to&thinsp;1"
    l: >-
      Informal evictions for every formal one. Most forced moves never reach
      a court.
    s: >-
      <a href="https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/periodicals/cityscpe/vol23num2/ch15.pdf">Gromis
      &amp; Desmond, Cityscape 2021</a>, 2017 AHS
  - v: "35"
    unit: "per&thinsp;100"
    l: >-
      Affordable and available rental homes per 100 extremely low-income
      renter households. The national shortage is 7.2 million homes.
    s: >-
      <a href="https://nlihc.org/gap">NLIHC, The Gap, March 2026</a>
  - v: "22.7"
    unit: "million"
    l: >-
      Renter households paying over 30% of income for housing in 2024. A
      record, and roughly half of all renters.
    s: >-
      <a href="https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2026.pdf">Harvard
      JCHS, America&#39;s Rental Housing 2026</a>
statnote: >-
  A filing count is the weakest number housing research publishes. It counts
  court cases, not displacement, and the 2017 American Housing Survey puts
  the national ratio at 5.5 informal evictions for every formal one. Where
  tenants have counsel and protections, more displacement passes through a
  court and gets counted. Where they do not, it disappears from the record.
  Every rate on this page carries that caveat.

framework:
  eyebrow: "The framework"
  h2_lead: "No single lever stops an eviction."
  h2_em: "It takes four."
  sub: >-
    ERN organizes the evidence as four P&#39;s, sorted by where each policy
    meets the problem (before the courthouse, inside it, or in the housing
    market underneath) and by how fast it acts. The further down the list,
    the slower the lever, and the more it addresses the cause rather than
    the case.
  tiles:
    - kicker: "01 · Prevent"
      href: "#prevent"
      body: >-
        Stop the case before it reaches court. Rental assistance, mediation,
        and time to pay resolve the debt instead of litigating it.
    - kicker: "02 · Protect"
      href: "#protect"
      body: >-
        Even the odds once a case exists. Counsel, sealed records, and a
        stated cause change what a filing costs a tenant.
    - kicker: "03 · Preserve"
      href: "#preserve"
      body: >-
        Keep the low-cost homes that already exist. They leave the market
        quietly, one sale or one expiring subsidy at a time.
    - kicker: "04 · Produce"
      href: "#produce"
      body: >-
        Add homes, especially below market. The slowest lever, and the only
        one that closes the shortage underneath the docket.
  note: >-
    Ordered by speed of effect: assistance lands in weeks, mediation in
    months, preservation and construction in years. The strongest single
    combination on the evidence pairs a Prevent tool (rental assistance)
    with a Protect tool (right to counsel). A fifth section names the floor
    under all four: the data, funding, and standing every lever depends on.

legend:
  heading: "How to read each plank"
  evidence: "the numbers in the plank were verified against the linked source"
  reasoned: "a logical case, argued from mechanism or arithmetic and labeled as such"
  tierkey: "Tier 1 = largest &amp; fastest effect &middot; Tier 3 = structural &amp; slow"

groups:
  - anchor: "prevent"
    num: "1"
    kicker: "01 · Prevent"
    h2_lead: "Nine in ten evicted tenants owe at least a month&#39;s rent."
    h2_em: "The fastest tools resolve the debt, not the tenancy."
    sub: >-
      Prevention acts before a case exists: pay the arrears, mediate the
      dispute, allow time to cure. The debts are small against the costs that
      follow. In the largest study of nonpayment cases, 90% of evicted
      tenants owed at least one month&#39;s rent, and across all tenants in
      the study the average balance at move-out was $1,252, about one and a
      quarter months&#39; rent
      (<a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w33155">Humphries et al., NBER
      2024</a>). The money goes to the landlord, the arrears clear, and no
      record is created.
    rows:
      - planks:
          - tier: "T1"
            tier_class: "t1"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-lapsed"
            status: "&#8856; Federal program ended"
            name: "Permanent emergency rental assistance"
            body: >-
              The pandemic ran the largest test of eviction prevention to
              date. Emergency Rental Assistance made nearly <strong>10.8
              million payments</strong> to households from $46.5 billion made
              available (<a href="https://home.treasury.gov/news/featured-stories/at-low-income-housing-forum-deputy-secretary-adeyemo-announces-nearly-108-million-emergency-rental-assistance-program-payments-to-families-at-risk-of-eviction">Treasury</a>),
              and with moratoria in force, 2021 filings ran at <strong>half
              their historical average</strong> in tracked areas
              (<a href="https://evictionlab.org/us-eviction-filing-patterns-2021/">Eviction
              Lab</a>). The HUD-funded evaluation by ERN and the Housing
              Initiative at Penn, spanning more than 700 counties in 22
              states, found that counties receiving more assistance saw fewer
              filings, with the largest effects where low-income renters,
              unemployment, and rent burden ran highest; assisted families in
              Los Angeles were <strong>53% less likely to have moved</strong>
              and 65% less likely to end up on the street, and among
              unfunded applicants who moved, a third reported the landlord
              forced them out with no court proceeding, against about 18% of
              funded applicants
              (<a href="https://evictionresearch.net/hud-era/">ERN &amp;
              Housing Initiative at Penn, 2026</a>). The design lesson
              carries to any successor: programs that verified eligibility
              with neighborhood-level data instead of pay stubs and hardship
              documents prevented more evictions.
              Minnesota has funded prevention assistance statewide since 1993
              (<a href="https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/462a.204">Minn.
              Stat. &sect; 462A.204</a>); in the year to September 2024,
              94% of households that received its prevention assistance
              kept their housing, a program exit figure rather than a
              counterfactual estimate
              (<a href="https://www.mnhousing.gov/documents/53609/fhpap-scoring-transparency_26-27/view">Minnesota
              Housing</a>). The plank is a standing national
              program that expands automatically when arrears rise, instead
              of one built from scratch in each emergency.
          - tier: "T1"
            tier_class: "t1"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Local models"
            name: "Divert the case before it reaches the docket"
            body: >-
              In Phase 2 of Philadelphia&#39;s diversion program,
              <strong>7.4%</strong> of cases that received rental assistance
              faced an eviction filing within six months, against
              <strong>42.2%</strong> without assistance, and 4.2% where the
              assistance came with a mediated agreement; over 21 months the
              assisted rate rose to 33.3%, a sign assistance sometimes
              delays rather than fully prevents
              (<a href="https://www.reinvestment.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Eviction-Diversion-Brief-11.29.23.pdf">Dowdall
              &amp; Goldstein, Reinvestment Fund 2023</a>). Philadelphia has
              required every landlord to enroll in the program and
              participate in good faith before filing since 2022, a rule
              made permanent in 2024 with a 30-day minimum
              (<a href="https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/philadelphia/latest/philadelphia_pa/0-0-0-278160">Phila.
              Code &sect; 9-811</a>). Washington State required pre-filing
              resolution statewide from November 2021, and the courts&#39;
              own evaluation found a <strong>78% settlement rate</strong>
              before the program ended in 2023
              (<a href="https://www.courts.wa.gov/newsinfo/pdf/ERPP%20Full%20Legislative%20Report%20to%20the%20Legislature.pdf">AOC
              legislative report</a>). Texas ran the model statewide through
              its Supreme Court and housing agency: courts paused cases
              while both parties applied, and more than 25,000 applicants
              received over $243 million (TDHCA, 2021&ndash;2023). Hawaii
              required mediation before any nonpayment filing in 2021 and
              2022, and its legal aid review found 85% of mediated tenants
              stayed housed
              (<a href="https://www.hawaiipublicradio.org/local-news/2022-10-19/report-mandatory-mediation-saved-hundreds-of-tenants-from-eviction">Hawaii
              Appleseed, as reported 2022</a>). Across 24 court-based
              programs in 17 states and D.C., <strong>89%</strong> of cases
              that engaged with diversion ended in a settlement or voluntary
              dismissal, and only 6% went to trial
              (<a href="https://www.ncsc.org/sites/default/files/media/document/EDI_Interim_Report_2024_3-18-25.pdf">National
              Center for State Courts, 2025</a>). The plank makes good-faith
              diversion a national precondition of filing.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; State models"
            name: "Slow the clock: notice, time to cure, a right to redeem"
            body: >-
              The statutory clock between falling behind and facing a filing
              decides whether assistance and mediation get the time they
              need. The cleanest natural experiment is Maryland, where for
              decades no notice was required, filing cost $15 (a fee the
              state raised in 2024), and trial came on the fifth day: Baltimore City alone recorded
              <strong>144,058 landlord-tenant filings</strong> in fiscal
              2017, thirty times the 4,788 in all of King County,
              Washington, a gap in process, not in hardship
              (<a href="https://mdcourts.gov/sites/default/files/import/publications/annualreport/reports/2017/fy2017statisticalabstract.pdf">Maryland
              Judiciary FY2017</a>; <em>Losing Home</em>, 2018). Maryland
              added a 10-day pre-filing notice in October 2021
              (<a href="https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2021RS/chapters_noln/Ch_746_hb0018E.pdf">Md.
              HB 18, Ch. 746</a>). In ERN&#39;s national
              eviction-risk model, two of the five strongest predictors of a
              neighborhood&#39;s filing rate, out of 184, are process
              clocks: the notice period and the post-judgment window
              (<a href="understanding-eviction.html">ERN, HPRM</a>).
              Washington State pairs a 14-day pay-or-vacate notice (SB 5600, 2019)
              with a statutory right to reinstate the tenancy by paying what
              is owed, before judgment or within five court days after
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.18.410">RCW
              59.18.410</a>); Minnesota adopted a 14-day pre-filing notice
              in 2024 and lets local governments set a longer one
              (<a href="https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/504B.321">Minn.
              Stat. &sect; 504B.321</a>). No study has yet isolated the
              effect of the notice length itself. Every redemption is an eviction that did not
              happen at a cost the tenant already owed. ERN&#39;s
              <a href="state-eviction-timeframes/">state timeframes
              table</a> compares all fifty states and D.C.; for the full
              process law from pre-filing through post-judgment, the Legal
              Services Corporation&#39;s
              <a href="https://www.lsc.gov/initiatives/effect-state-local-laws-evictions/lsc-eviction-laws-database">Eviction
              Laws Database</a>, built with Temple&#39;s Center for Public
              Health Law Research, covers every state and territory as a
              snapshot of law in effect January 1, 2021.
      - planks:
          - tier: "T1"
            tier_class: "t1"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Programs, not a guarantee"
            name: "Fund homelessness prevention like the returns are real"
            body: >-
              Families who called Chicago&#39;s homelessness-prevention line
              when one-time emergency funds happened to be available were
              <strong>76% less likely</strong> to enter a homeless shelter
              within six months than families who called when funds were
              not, at roughly
              <strong>$10,300 per instance of homelessness averted</strong>
              (<a href="https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aag0833">Evans,
              Sullivan &amp; Wallskog, <em>Science</em> 2016</a>). A Santa
              Clara County randomized trial of prevention assistance
              returned an estimated <strong>$2.47 in benefits for every
              dollar spent</strong>
              (<a href="https://leo.nd.edu/news/santa-clara-county-homelessness-prevention/">Phillips
              &amp; Sullivan, 2023</a>). Chronic homelessness costs the
              public roughly <strong>$35,000 per person per year</strong>
              (National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2017). Prevention
              spends four figures per household; homelessness costs five
              figures per person per year. The populations differ, so this
              is a comparison of magnitudes, not a one-to-one ledger.
          - tier: "T1"
            tier_class: "t1"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Programs, not a right"
            name: "Permanent housing for people experiencing homelessness"
            body: >-
              On a single night in January 2025, <strong>745,652
              people</strong> were homeless in the United States
              (<a href="https://www.hud.gov/news/hud-no-26-037">HUD 2025
              AHAR</a>). The evidence for permanent supportive housing is
              strong exactly where a housing policy needs it. It maintains
              housing stability for most chronically homeless people over
              the studied one-to-two-year windows, while the National
              Academies found no substantial evidence yet that it improves
              health outcomes, and this page keeps that distinction
              (<a href="https://nap.nationalacademies.org/resource/25133/Permanent%20Supportive%20Housing-ReportHighlights.pdf">NASEM
              2018</a>). For homeless families, a long-term rent subsidy cut
              subsequent homelessness by more than half against usual care
              (<a href="https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/family-options-study-full-report.pdf">HUD
              Family Options Study, 2016</a>). The plank funds permanent
              housing at the scale of the count and evaluates it on the
              outcome it demonstrably moves.

  - anchor: "protect"
    num: "2"
    kicker: "02 · Protect"
    h2_lead: "Landlords arrive with a lawyer 84% of the time."
    h2_em: "Tenants, 4%."
    sub: >-
      Protection changes what happens once a case exists: who has a lawyer,
      what the record does afterward, and whether a tenancy can end without a
      stated reason. None of it prevents the filing; all of it changes what
      the filing costs.
    rows:
      - planks:
          - tier: "T1"
            tier_class: "t1"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; States and cities, no federal right"
            name: "A right to counsel in eviction court"
            body: >-
              Absent a right to counsel, about <strong>4% of
              tenants</strong> have lawyers against <strong>84% of
              landlords</strong>, the National Coalition for a Civil Right
              to Counsel&#39;s average across several dozen local studies.
              <strong>28 jurisdictions</strong> (5 states, 21 cities, 2
              counties) have enacted some version of the right
              (<a href="https://civilrighttocounsel.org/resources/organizing_around_right_to_counsel/">NCCRC,
              August 2026</a>); Washington State&#39;s 2021 law was the first
              statewide
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.18.640">RCW
              59.18.640</a>), with Maryland and Connecticut following the
              same year. The results are measured. In New York City,
              <strong>84%</strong> of households represented in court
              remained in their homes in FY2023
              (<a href="https://www.nyc.gov/assets/hra/downloads/pdf/services/civiljustice/OCJ_UA_Annual_Report_2023.pdf">Office
              of Civil Justice</a>); in Cleveland, represented clients with
              a legal defense prevented an eviction or involuntary move
              <strong>83%</strong> of the time in 2025
              (<a href="https://www.stout.com/-/media/pdf/evictions/stout2025independentevaluationclevelandevictionrightcounselfinal20260129.pdf">Stout
              independent evaluation, 2026</a>). Statewide programs show
              the same pattern: Connecticut&#39;s attorneys helped clients
              avoid disruptive displacement in <strong>85%</strong> of cases
              and returned an estimated $3.65 per dollar spent
              (<a href="https://www.stout.com/-/media/pdf/evictions/stout-year-4-ct-rtc-independent-evaluation-final-2025-12-23.pdf">Stout,
              2025</a>), and Maryland&#39;s program kept 88% of clients who
              wanted to stay in their homes, at $3.04 per dollar
              (<a href="https://oag.maryland.gov/News/Pages/Groundbreaking-Access-to-Counsel-in-Evictions-Program-(ACE)-Delivers-Significant-Impact-for-Maryland-Tenants.aspx">Maryland
              Attorney General, 2025</a>). Counsel also answers the
              default problem: across New York State&#39;s covered
              jurisdictions, 54% of nonpayment filings went unanswered by
              the tenant, and defaults account for an estimated 40% of the
              eviction warrants issued across the state
              (<a href="https://furmancenter.org/files/publications/Half_the_Battle_is_Just_Showing_Up_V3_(1).pdf">NYU
              Furman Center, 2023</a>). A 2018 Stout analysis for Philadelphia
              projected roughly <strong>$12.74 returned for every
              dollar</strong> spent on tenant counsel. The plank is a
              national right, funded like the public-defender obligation it
              parallels.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Some states"
            name: "Just cause to end a tenancy"
            body: >-
              A just-cause standard ends no-cause terminations, so a tenancy
              can be ended only for a listed reason. New Jersey has required
              good cause since 1974, a law its legislature tied to the
              state&#39;s housing shortage (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1); Oregon and
              California adopted statewide standards in 2019
              (<a href="https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2019R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/SB608/Enrolled">SB
              608</a>; AB 1482), Washington State in 2021
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.18.650">RCW
              59.18.650</a>), and Colorado and New York in 2024. The CARB anti-displacement review rates
              just-cause protections <strong>high-potential and
              fast-acting</strong>
              (<a href="https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/19RD018%20-%20Anti-Displacement%20Strategy%20Effectiveness.pdf">Chapple
              &amp; Loukaitou-Sideris, 2021</a>). The direct effect is
              definitional, ending no-cause terminations; causal estimates
              of the effect on filings are thinner than for the tools above,
              and this page treats that as an open question rather than
              settled. The plank sets a national floor while leaving the
              list of causes to the states.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Some states"
            name: "Make voucher discrimination illegal everywhere"
            body: >-
              A voucher only prevents an eviction if a landlord will take
              it. In HUD&#39;s five-city paired-testing study, landlords
              refused voucher holders in <strong>78%</strong> of tests in
              Fort Worth, 76% in Los Angeles, and 67% in Philadelphia,
              against 31% in Newark and 15% in Washington, D.C. The
              study&#39;s own summary is that landlord refusal is more
              common in jurisdictions without source-of-income protections,
              though it did not evaluate the laws&#39; impact
              (<a href="https://www.urban.org/research/publication/pilot-study-landlord-acceptance-housing-choice-vouchers">Cunningham
              et al., Urban Institute for HUD, 2018</a>). Adoption has
              spread far enough that PRRAC estimates it is likely that over
              <strong>60%</strong> of voucher holders are now covered by a
              state or local law
              (<a href="https://www.prrac.org/pdf/AppendixB.pdf">Appendix B,
              updated March 2026</a>). Refusing a tenant because rent
              arrives as a voucher wastes money the public has already
              committed. The plank adds source of income to federal
              fair-housing law, so protection stops depending on the state
              line.
      - planks:
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; 19 states and D.C."
            name: "Seal the record until the case has merit"
            body: >-
              Screening reports recite any filing regardless of outcome,
              and the Fair Credit Reporting Act lets a civil record ride a
              report for up to seven years
              (<a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681c">15
              U.S.C. &sect; 1681c</a>). Roughly <strong>22%</strong> of
              eviction records carry ambiguous information on how the case
              was resolved or falsely represent a tenant&#39;s history
              (<a href="https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/inaccuracies-in-eviction-records-implications-for-renters-and-res/">Porton,
              Gromis &amp; Desmond, <em>Housing Policy Debate</em> 2021</a>),
              landlords in a behavioral experiment treated mere filings like
              executed evictions
              (<a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10511482.2022.2113815">So,
              <em>Housing Policy Debate</em> 2023</a>), and the CFPB logged
              more than <strong>16,000</strong> renter complaints about
              incorrect information on screening reports
              (<a href="https://www.consumerfinance.gov/about-us/newsroom/cfpb-reports-highlight-problems-with-tenant-background-checks/">2022</a>).
              Black renters are <strong>19.9%</strong> of adult renters and
              <strong>32.7%</strong> of eviction-filing defendants
              (<a href="https://sociologicalscience.com/articles-v7-27-649/">Hepburn,
              Louis &amp; Desmond, <em>Sociological Science</em> 2020</a>),
              which is why blanket record screening draws disparate-impact
              challenges under the Fair Housing Act; the first such case, by
              the ACLU&#39;s account, was brought for a tenant whose
              years-old filing never resulted in an eviction (<em>Smith v. Wasatch</em>, W.D. Wash. 2017, built on
              ERN&#39;s King County analysis). Nineteen states and D.C. have
              passed sealing or expungement policies
              (<a href="https://nlihc.org/sites/default/files/AG-2026/CH7/2_Eviction_Record_Sealing_Expungement_Chapter_7.pdf">NLIHC,
              2026</a>), and NLIHC&#39;s
              <a href="https://nlihc.org/tenant-protections">State and
              Local Tenant Protections Database</a> tracks adoption
              jurisdiction by jurisdiction. California hides every filing from the general
              public by default and unmasks it only if the landlord wins
              within 60 days of filing, or later by court order
              (<a href="https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1161.2.&amp;lawCode=CCP">CCP
              &sect; 1161.2</a>); Massachusetts lets tenants seal no-fault
              cases at any time, nonpayment cases after four years, and
              dismissals or tenant wins without a hearing
              (<a href="https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartIII/TitleIII/Chapter239/Section16">G.L.
              c. 239, &sect; 16</a>, 2024); Washington State seals case by
              case, at the court&#39;s discretion
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.18.367">RCW
              59.18.367</a>). The plank is the California default,
              nationally.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-none"
            status: "&#9675; Largely unaddressed"
            name: "Price serial filing out of the collections business"
            body: >-
              In 2014, nearly <strong>one in three</strong> households
              facing eviction nationally was filed against more than once
              (Leung, Hepburn &amp; Desmond, <em>Social Forces</em> 2020),
              and serial filing runs highest where filing is cheap and
              fast. A 2023 study ties every <strong>$76</strong> of filing
              fee to a <strong>3.11-point drop</strong> in serial filing
              (Gomory et al., <em>Housing Policy Debate</em> 2023; both via
              the
              <a href="https://www.networkforphl.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Deterring-Serial-Eviction-Filing.pdf">Network
              for Public Health Law fact sheet, 2025</a>). The plank pairs meaningful filing fees with
              limits on repeat filings against the same household, so the
              courthouse stops functioning as a rent-collection window.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; One state, local bans, federal consent judgment"
            name: "Ban algorithmic rent collusion"
            body: >-
              Rent-setting software that pools competitors&#39; private data
              lets landlords coordinate increases no one would risk alone.
              The Department of Justice sued RealPage in 2024, and a
              consent judgment entered in May 2026 requires the software to
              stop using competitors&#39; nonpublic data to set rents; the
              states&#39; claims against RealPage and several large landlords
              continued past a September 2026 ruling
              (<a href="https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-requires-realpage-end-sharing-competitively-sensitive-information-and">DOJ</a>;
              <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-05-08/pdf/2026-09147.pdf">Federal
              Register</a>). New York enacted the first statewide ban in
              October 2025, making it unlawful to run or license software
              that coordinates rents between landlords
              (<a href="https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S7882">S.
              7882, Ch. 437</a>); Seattle banned the practice in 2025
              (<a href="https://library.municode.com/wa/seattle/codes/municipal_code?nodeId=TIT7CO_CH7.34PRRESEALSOSE">SMC
              7.34</a>) and King County followed for its unincorporated
              areas. The plank writes the same rule into national law, so it
              stops depending on case-by-case enforcement.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Some states"
            name: "Anti-gouging rent stabilization, designed not to chill building"
            body: >-
              Second-generation caps limit increases inside a tenancy while
              exempting new construction, which is where the supply risk
              lives. Oregon set the first statewide cap in 2019, at 7 points
              plus inflation with a 15-year new-construction exemption
              (<a href="https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2019R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/SB608/Enrolled">SB
              608</a>, since tightened to a 10% ceiling); California
              followed the same year at 5 points plus inflation, capped at
              10% (AB 1482); Washington State&#39;s 2025 law caps increases
              at 7 points plus inflation to a maximum of 10%
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.18.700">RCW
              59.18.700</a>), with a 12-year new-construction exemption
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.18.710">RCW
              59.18.710</a>). The
              honest evidence cuts both ways. San Francisco&#39;s 1994
              expansion cut its rental supply about <strong>15%</strong>,
              with landlords converting buildings to condos and redeveloping
              them rather than cutting new construction, under a law that
              also exempted new building
              (<a href="https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20181289">Diamond,
              McQuade &amp; Qian, <em>AER</em> 2019</a>). Rent
              regulation is a stability tool, not a supply tool, and the
              new-construction exemption is its single most protective
              design feature. The plank is a national anti-gouging ceiling
              of that second-generation design, not a hard freeze.

  - anchor: "preserve"
    num: "3"
    kicker: "03 · Preserve"
    h2_lead: "2.5 million of the cheapest rentals left the market in a decade."
    h2_em: "No court recorded it."
    sub: >-
      Preservation keeps existing low-cost homes on the market: the aging
      private stock that rents cheap, and the subsidized stock whose
      affordability runs on a contract clock. Losses here displace people
      without any legal event, which ERN measures as soft displacement, so
      the harm never appears in a court record.
    rows:
      - planks:
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Funded, oversubscribed"
            name: "A national fund for the unsubsidized low-cost stock"
            body: >-
              Between 2014 and 2024 the country lost <strong>9.3
              million</strong> units renting under $1,400 a month; 2.5
              million of them rented under $600, a <strong>30%
              decrease</strong> in the lowest-cost stock in one decade
              (<a href="https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2026.pdf">JCHS,
              <em>America&#39;s Rental Housing 2026</em></a>). No eviction
              is filed when a building leaves the low-cost market; the
              households that would have lived there never appear in any
              record. About <strong>three quarters</strong> of Americans in
              affordable housing live in unsubsidized units, and the CARB
              review rates preserving them among the highest-potential
              anti-displacement strategies, effective in any market and fast
              (<a href="https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/19RD018%20-%20Anti-Displacement%20Strategy%20Effectiveness.pdf">Chapple
              &amp; Loukaitou-Sideris, 2021</a>). Where funds exist they are
              swamped: Washington State&#39;s 2026 preservation round drew
              <strong>$97.7 million in requests against $34.1 million
              available</strong>
              (<a href="https://www.commerce.wa.gov/commerce-receives-91-applications-for-preservation-and-continuing-affordability-of-multifamily-housing/">Commerce,
              May 2026</a>). The plank is a standing federal acquisition
              fund sized to the demand states already demonstrate.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; DC and manufactured-home states"
            name: "A first chance for tenants to buy the building"
            body: >-
              Under Washington, D.C.&#39;s tenant opportunity-to-purchase law,
              <strong>58%</strong> of tenants in one study sample made it
              through the purchase process and could afford their units in
              the end (Gallaher 2016, via the
              <a href="https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/19RD018%20-%20Anti-Displacement%20Strategy%20Effectiveness.pdf">CARB
              white paper</a>), and a 2023 review counted 16,224 affordable
              homes developed or preserved under the law between 1975 and
              2021
              (<a href="https://cnhed.org/news/cnhed-releases-comprehensive-analysis-of-dcs-tenant-opportunity-to-purchase-act-topa/">CNHED</a>).
              Washington State requires notice before a
              manufactured-home community is marketed for sale and gives
              residents 70 days to form an organization and declare their
              intent to compete, an opportunity to compete rather than a
              right of first refusal
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.20.325">RCW
              59.20.325</a>). The plank is a national notice-and-opportunity
              floor for any sale of an occupied rental property, with
              financing to make tenant and nonprofit bids real. PolicyLink
              publishes a policy brief on
              <a href="https://policylink.org/resources-tools/tools/all-in-cities/housing-anti-displacement/topa-copa">tenant
              and community opportunity to purchase</a> in its All-In
              Cities toolkit.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; State patchwork"
            name: "Protect the homes people own on land they rent"
            body: >-
              A manufactured home is the largest unsubsidized
              affordable-housing stock in the country&#39;s rural counties,
              and its owner is uniquely exposed. The home is theirs, the
              ground is not, and moving the home is often impossible in
              practice. Washington State caps lot-rent increases at 5%
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.20.370">RCW
              59.20.370</a>) with three months&#39; notice of any increase
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.20.090">RCW
              59.20.090</a>); its
              sale-notice law names community land trusts among the
              eligible buyers
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.20.030">RCW
              59.20.030</a>). Minnesota requires 45 days&#39; notice before
              a park is sold to a converter, lets residents match the price,
              and pays relocation costs from a state trust fund when a park
              closes
              (<a href="https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/327C.095">Minn.
              Stat. &sect; 327C.095</a>). The plank is a national floor of
              lot-rent protection, sale notice, and purchase financing for
              resident ownership. The logic is exposure. Rules written for
              tenants and rules written for owners both miss the household
              that is each on one side of the property line.
      - planks:
          - tier: "T3"
            tier_class: "t3"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Local, narrow reach"
            name: "Community control of land"
            body: >-
              Community land trusts take land off the private market for
              good. The CARB review rates their displacement-prevention
              potential <strong>high</strong> and, unlike new construction,
              they do not need a hot market to work; the same review finds
              them rare, dependent on coordinated tenant action and economic
              resources, and generally not reaching the lowest incomes
              (<a href="https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/19RD018%20-%20Anti-Displacement%20Strategy%20Effectiveness.pdf">Chapple
              &amp; Loukaitou-Sideris, 2021</a>). The plank funds
              acquisition at a scale that changes that last finding.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-yes"
            status: "&#10003; Federal law, floor set high"
            name: "Lower the ceiling on corporate single-family ownership"
            body: >-
              Federal law, in force from January 2027, bars an investor
              holding <strong>350 or more</strong> single-family homes from
              buying another, with exceptions and no divestment requirement
              (<a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ101/pdf/PLAW-119publ101.pdf">21st
              Century ROAD to Housing Act</a>, Public Law 119&ndash;101,
              2026). The eviction link is measured. In Fulton County,
              Georgia, large corporate owners of single-family rentals were
              <strong>8% more likely</strong> than small landlords to file
              eviction notices, after controls
              (<a href="https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/historical/frbatl/publications/ceddps/frbatl_discussionpaper_2016-4.pdf">Raymond
              et al., Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, 2016</a>). The
              plank lowers the threshold toward the 100-home lines states
              are already debating, and adds beneficial-ownership disclosure
              so the count cannot hide behind shell LLCs.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-none"
            status: "&#9675; No standing renewal fund"
            name: "Renew the affordability the public already bought"
            body: >-
              Five million rental homes, one in ten rentals nationally,
              carry federally funded project-based subsidies, and
              affordability restrictions are set to expire on
              <strong>374,497</strong> of them by 2028
              (<a href="https://preservationdatabase.org/picture-of-preservation/">NLIHC
              &amp; PAHRC, <em>2024 Picture of Preservation</em></a>). When an
              owner opts out, the affordability ends without a single court
              event, and the public usually buys the same affordability
              twice somewhere else. At-risk properties are tracked one by
              one in the National Housing Preservation Database. The plank
              is a standing renewal fund plus a first right to purchase for
              mission-driven buyers whenever a subsidized property&#39;s
              restrictions approach expiration. Renewing a home the public
              already financed is the cheapest unit the public will ever
              add.

  - anchor: "produce"
    num: "4"
    kicker: "04 · Produce"
    h2_lead: "35 affordable homes exist for every 100 of the lowest-income renters."
    h2_em: "Nothing above closes that gap."
    sub: >-
      Production is the slowest lever and the only structural one: every tool
      above operates inside a shortage that none of them reduces. Its
      evidence runs through rents and exposure rather than courtrooms. New
      supply lowers nearby rents, and rent burden is where eviction risk
      concentrates.
    rows:
      - planks:
          - tier: "T3"
            tier_class: "t3"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; State reforms spreading"
            name: "Build more homes, of every kind"
            body: >-
              Large new market-rate buildings in low-income areas lower
              nearby rents by <strong>5 to 7 percent</strong> relative to
              comparable areas, and draw more in-movers from lower-income
              neighborhoods, the reverse of the displacement usually feared
              (Asquith, Mast &amp; Reed, <em>REStat</em> 2023). The chain is
              measured: a new market-rate building housing 100 people leads
              <strong>45 to 70 people</strong> to move out of
              below-median-income neighborhoods, most within three years
              (<a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0094119021000656">Mast,
              <em>JUE</em> 2023</a>). City-scale reforms show the same
              direction. Auckland upzoned about three quarters of its
              residential land in 2016; eight years on, rents were an
              estimated <strong>23% below</strong> the no-reform
              counterfactual
              (<a href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ecin.70075">Greenaway-McGrevy
              &amp; So, <em>Economic Inquiry</em> 2026</a>) after a
              construction boom the reform demonstrably stimulated
              (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jue.2023.103555">Greenaway-McGrevy
              &amp; Phillips, <em>JUE</em> 2023</a>). Minneapolis grew its
              stock <strong>12%</strong> from 2017 to 2022 after its
              land-use reforms while rents rose 1%; the rest of Minnesota
              added 4% and rents rose 14%
              (<a href="https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2024/01/04/minneapolis-land-use-reforms-offer-a-blueprint-for-housing-affordability">Pew,
              2024</a>). The pipeline is currently shrinking: multifamily
              starts fell from a three-decade peak of 547,000 units in 2022
              to 416,000 in 2025
              (<a href="https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2026.pdf">JCHS
              2026</a>). The plank ties federal infrastructure money
              to a statewide zoning floor that legalizes middle housing,
              with Washington State&#39;s package as the model.
          - tier: "T3"
            tier_class: "t3"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-none"
            status: "&#9675; Far short everywhere"
            name: "Build the homes the market never builds"
            body: >-
              The national shortage is <strong>7.2 million</strong> rental
              homes affordable and available to the country&#39;s 11
              million extremely low-income renter households; only 35 exist
              per 100 such households, and <strong>74%</strong> of those
              renters spend more than half their income on rent and
              utilities (<a href="https://nlihc.org/gap">NLIHC, The Gap,
              2026</a>). Across cities, homelessness tracks housing-market
              conditions, absolute rent levels and vacancy rates, more than
              it tracks local poverty, addiction, or weather
              (<a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/homelessness-is-a-housing-problem/paper">Colburn
              &amp; Aldern, <em>Homelessness Is a Housing Problem</em>,
              2022</a>).
              The market cannot price a home an extremely low-income renter
              can pay, because the rent that household can afford does not
              cover the cost of operating the building, let alone
              constructing it. Deep affordability exists only where the
              public builds it or buys it. The plank is a production
              program targeted at 0&ndash;30% of area median income, sized
              against the 7.2 million gap. No prevention or protection tool
              changes that arithmetic.
          - tier: "T3"
            tier_class: "t3"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Local experiments"
            name: "Social housing that pays for itself"
            body: >-
              Publicly developed mixed-income housing, where higher rents
              cross-subsidize lower ones, is standard practice in much of
              the world and newly live in the United States. Seattle voters
              created a social housing developer in 2023 and funded it in
              2025 with a 5% payroll tax on compensation above $1 million,
              estimated at roughly <strong>$53 million a year</strong>
              (<a href="https://nlihc.org/resource/seattle-voters-approve-ballot-initiative-fund-social-housing-developer">Proposition
              1A</a>). The plank is a federal revolving loan fund that lets
              any city capitalize a developer like it once, then recycle the
              money. The logic is a balance sheet. A public developer
              borrows once, builds, and repays from rents, so a dollar
              produces homes repeatedly instead of subsidizing once.
      - planks:
          - tier: "T3"
            tier_class: "t3"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; State models"
            name: "Public land for public homes"
            body: >-
              Governments already own land in the places homes are
              scarcest. Washington State lets any agency transfer surplus public
              property for affordable housing on any mutually agreeable
              terms, including at no cost, with a covenant binding the use
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=39.33.015">RCW
              39.33.015</a>), and requires counties to offer tax-foreclosed
              parcels to the city for affordable housing before auction
              (<a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=36.35.150">RCW
              36.35.150</a>). The plank is a federal
              default. Surplus public land is offered for permanently
              affordable housing before anything else, priced at its use,
              not its speculation.
          - tier: "T3"
            tier_class: "t3"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; State models, oversubscribed"
            name: "Turn renters into owners, and count the vacancy it creates"
            body: >-
              Every renter who buys leaves a rental behind, so ownership
              programs are rental-supply policy too; the chain breaks only
              where the purchase itself displaces a sitting tenant. That
              much is arithmetic, not a study. Washington State&#39;s
              Covenant Homeownership Program lends <strong>0%-interest
              down-payment assistance</strong> to first-time buyers from
              communities harmed by racially restrictive covenants, funded
              by a $100 recording fee projected to raise $75&ndash;100
              million a year; demand already outpaces its monthly funds
              (<a href="https://heretohome.org/covenant">HB 1474, 2023</a>).
              HUD opened a Fair Housing Act investigation of the program in
              March 2026, which is unresolved.
              The plank is a national down-payment program with a
              repair-the-harm design, sized to its own waiting lists.
          - tier: "T3"
            tier_class: "t3"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Rated, not yet funded to scale"
            name: "Trade density and tax breaks for below-market homes"
            body: >-
              Inclusionary and incentive tools depend on a strong market;
              the CARB review rates them medium-potential and long-term
              (<a href="https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/19RD018%20-%20Anti-Displacement%20Strategy%20Effectiveness.pdf">Chapple
              &amp; Loukaitou-Sideris, 2021</a>). Washington State&#39;s
              transit-density law attaches 50-year affordability strings to
              its upzones. The plank keeps the trade honest nationally.
              Public value created by public rezoning buys permanent
              affordability, not a one-cycle discount.

  - anchor: "floor"
    num: "5"
    kicker: "05 · The floor"
    h2_lead: "The best national count still misses a million cases a year."
    h2_em: "Every lever above stands on this floor."
    sub: >-
      Four levers, one foundation: data that shows whether any of this
      works, assistance that does not run out mid-year, and the standing to
      invoke a right without losing your home for trying. Two of these
      planks are measured; four are labeled as the reasoned arguments they
      are.
    rows:
      - planks:
          - tier: "T1"
            tier_class: "t1"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Six states publish; no federal count"
            name: "Count every eviction"
            body: >-
              The federal government&#39;s own review concluded that
              "relatively little comprehensive data exist on evictions in
              the U.S."
              (<a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-106637">GAO-24-106637,
              2024</a>), and the best national estimates, built from 99.9
              million collected court records, still undercount filings by
              about <strong>1 million cases a year</strong> because some
              counties&#39; records cannot be obtained
              (<a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2116169119">Gromis
              et al., PNAS 2022</a>). In ERN&#39;s 50-state census of
              eviction data sources, only six jurisdictions (Alaska,
              Connecticut, DC, Maryland, New York, Virginia) publish
              statewide case-level eviction data. California will join
              them: SB 1160, which directs the Judicial Council to collect
              and publish eviction case data from every county, was signed
              on September 27, 2026 (Chapter 681, Statutes of 2026), with
              reporting phased in over the following years
              (<a href="https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB1160">leginfo</a>).
              The plank is a national eviction data
              standard. Courts report standardized, outcome-complete case
              data the way public health reports disease. Nothing else on
              this page can be evaluated without it.
          - tier: "T1"
            tier_class: "t1"
            ev_class: "ev-e"
            ev_label: "Evidence"
            status_class: "s-none"
            status: "&#9675; Rationed by lottery and line"
            name: "Make rental assistance an entitlement, not a lottery"
            body: >-
              Federal rental assistance reaches <strong>5.1
              million</strong> households, and <strong>3 in 4</strong>
              eligible households receive none of it
              (<a href="https://www.cbpp.org/research/housing/policy-basics-federal-rental-assistance">CBPP,
              2026</a>). Eviction is not only a hardship; it is a cause of
              the harms that follow it. A study using cases randomly
              assigned to judges across Cook County and New York courts
              found an eviction order raised shelter use by <strong>3.4
              percentage points</strong>, an increase of more than
              <strong>300%</strong>, cut earnings about <strong>14%</strong>
              by the second year, and raised hospital visits
              <strong>29%</strong>, with the housing and labor effects
              concentrated among female and Black tenants
              (<a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w30382">Collinson et
              al., <em>QJE</em> 2024</a>). And when voucher families in the
              Creating Moves to Opportunity experiment received customized
              search help, landlord outreach, and short-term financial
              assistance, the share moving to high-upward-mobility
              neighborhoods rose from <strong>15% to 53%</strong>
              (<a href="https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20200407">Bergman
              et al., <em>AER</em> 2024</a>). The plank phases federal
              rental assistance toward an entitlement for eligible
              households, paired with the search help that makes a voucher
              a real choice.
      - planks:
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-none"
            status: "&#9675; Nowhere yet"
            name: "Subsidy parity for renters"
            body: >-
              Federal tax law subsidizes owning a home as a standing
              entitlement, no waiting list attached. Assistance for renting
              one is rationed. The plank is a renter&#39;s tax credit that
              closes part of that gap for cost-burdened households. The
              logic is symmetry. If housing is worth subsidizing through
              the tax code, tenure should not decide who gets the subsidy.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-none"
            status: "&#9675; No general national right"
            name: "A right to organize without retaliation"
            body: >-
              Every protection on this page is enforced, in practice, by a
              tenant willing to invoke it, and retaliation is how
              invocation gets suppressed. Labor law solved the same problem
              a century ago by protecting the organizing itself. The plank
              is a national right to form and join tenant associations,
              with retaliation for organizing treated the way retaliation
              for union activity is treated. The logic is enforcement.
              Rights that depend on isolated individuals asserting them
              against their own landlord under-enforce by design.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-local"
            status: "&#9681; Complaint-driven almost everywhere"
            name: "A habitability floor someone actually inspects"
            body: >-
              Habitability standards exist nearly everywhere and are
              enforced almost nowhere, because enforcement waits for a
              tenant complaint, and complaining invites the eviction the
              rest of this page is about. The plank pairs a national
              habitability floor with proactive rental inspection and
              registration, shifting enforcement from the household with
              the least power to the government with the most. The logic is
              incentives. A standard enforced only by its most vulnerable
              beneficiary is a standard designed to be waived. PolicyLink
              publishes a policy brief on
              <a href="https://www.policylink.org/resources-tools/tools/all-in-cities/housing-anti-displacement/rental-registries">rental
              registries</a>, the registration half of this plank.
          - tier: "T2"
            tier_class: "t2"
            ev_class: "ev-r"
            ev_label: "Reasoned"
            status_class: "s-none"
            status: "&#9675; Owner-centric by design"
            name: "Rehouse renters after disasters like owners"
            body: >-
              Disaster recovery is built around the property owner.
              Rebuilding aid follows the deed, and the renter displaced
              from the same address holds a thinner claim on a shorter
              clock. Climate change is making displacement without an
              eviction filing a growing share of all displacement, and none
              of it appears in court data. The plank writes tenure-neutral
              rehousing into disaster law. Displacement is measured by who
              lost their home, not by who owned it.

closing:
  thruline:
    - >-
      <strong>The pandemic ran the experiment no legislature would have
      authorized.</strong> For about two years the country operated several
      of these planks at once, a filing moratorium and $46.5 billion in
      emergency rental assistance, and 2021 filings ran at half their
      historical average, with more than three million cases avoided
      between March 2020 and the end of 2021
      (<a href="https://evictionlab.org/us-eviction-filing-patterns-2021/">Eviction
      Lab</a>). Filings returned as each piece lapsed. The lesson is not
      that emergencies work. It is that these levers move the number, and
      that no state holds all four at once.
    - >-
      <strong>The costs of doing nothing are measured.</strong> An eviction
      filing that never reaches a judgment is associated with 19% higher
      mortality, and an eviction judgment with 40%
      (<a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10828546/">Graetz
      et al., <em>Social Science &amp; Medicine</em> 2024</a>). Eviction
      during pregnancy is associated with lower birth weight and more
      premature births
      (<a href="https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2776776">Himmelstein
      &amp; Desmond, <em>JAMA Pediatrics</em> 2021</a>). These are
      associations measured on millions of records, and they fall on the
      same households the screening, filing, and shortage planks above
      describe.
    - >-
      <strong>The pair that works is a lawyer and a check.</strong>
      Cleveland&#39;s right-to-counsel evaluation shows the mechanism.
      About half of eviction cases carry no legal defense, and those cases,
      in the evaluator&#39;s words, "center on the amount of back rent
      owed, which often requires a monetary solution." In 2025, represented
      clients with a legal defense prevented an eviction or involuntary
      move 83% of the time; clients without one, 70%. The program&#39;s
      prevention rate for 2025 cases, 76%, sat below its 83% since 2020,
      in the year the county&#39;s rental assistance programs closed
      (<a href="https://www.stout.com/-/media/pdf/evictions/stout2025independentevaluationclevelandevictionrightcounselfinal20260129.pdf">Stout,
      2026</a>). A lawyer wins the case with a legal defect. A check
      resolves the case without one. National policy funds both,
      permanently, and measures the result with data it finally collects.
  callout:
    heading: "What we know"
    body: >-
      What works is no longer the open question. A decade of evaluations
      points the same way. Rental assistance, diversion, representation,
      and record sealing all show measured results, and several return more
      than they cost. The open questions are implementation and speed:
      whether a jurisdiction is willing and able to adopt and fund what is
      proven, and how to keep people housed while the slow levers catch up.
      Where the evidence on eviction specifically is mixed or indirect,
      each plank says so on its face rather than rounding up. For the full
      literature, see the <a href="research.html#library">research
      library</a>. For a tailored briefing on any plank,
      <a href="mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu?Subject=Policy%20briefing%20request">contact ERN</a>.
  method: >-
    How this list was made: every plank marked <strong>Evidence</strong>
    carries direct, quantified findings of reduced eviction filings,
    judgments, or displacement, or of a measurably changed case cost, from
    peer-reviewed studies, federal evaluations, statutes, and program
    records, linked in place. Each was verified against the named source in
    August 2026 and checked again in October 2026. Planks marked <strong>Reasoned</strong> are argued from
    mechanism or arithmetic and labeled as such rather than dressed up as
    findings. Where the evidence is thin or cuts both ways, the plank says
    so. The four-P framing is ERN&#39;s, and the plank structure is shared
    with ERN&#39;s draft national housing rights charter. For how eviction
    itself works (the process, the records, the data), see
    <a href="understanding-eviction.html">Understanding Eviction</a>; for
    the full literature, the <a href="research.html#library">research
    library</a>; for the adoption trackers and drafting libraries other
    organizations maintain, <a href="#shelf">the reference shelf</a> at
    the foot of this page.

## The reference shelf {#shelf}

This page grades the evidence behind each plank. Four companion resources,
maintained by other organizations, track what this page does not: which
jurisdictions have adopted what, how the legal process runs in each state,
and how to draft the ordinance. ERN links them here because a legislator's
next question after "does it work" is "who has it, and what does the bill
say."

- **[State and Local Tenant Protections Database](https://nlihc.org/tenant-protections)**,
  National Low Income Housing Coalition. Tracks right to counsel, source-of-income
  protection, eviction record sealing, anti-rent-gouging measures, and just-cause
  laws across states, territories, tribes, and localities, with comprehensive
  tracking since January 2021. The live answer to where any Protect plank stands
  in your jurisdiction.
- **[Eviction Laws Database](https://www.lsc.gov/initiatives/effect-state-local-laws-evictions/lsc-eviction-laws-database)**,
  Legal Services Corporation, with the Center for Public Health Law Research
  at Temple University. Maps the legal process of eviction from pre-filing
  through post-judgment for all fifty states, D.C., and the U.S. territories,
  plus a 30-jurisdiction local sample. A snapshot of law in effect January 1,
  2021, which makes it the baseline against which the protections passed since
  can be read; ERN's [state timeframes table](state-eviction-timeframes/)
  carries the current process clocks.
- **[Housing Policy Library](https://www.housingsolutionslab.org/housing-policy-library/)**,
  Housing Solutions Lab at the NYU Furman Center, originally built as the
  Local Housing Solutions toolkit. Implementation briefs across the full
  breadth of local housing policy, organized on four pillars of its own
  (dedicated affordable units, housing supply, access to private-market homes,
  and protection against displacement and poor conditions). The drafting-level
  detail this page leaves to the bill writers.
- **[All-In Cities Anti-Displacement Toolkit](https://www.policylink.org/resources-tools/tools/all-in-cities/housing-anti-displacement)**,
  PolicyLink. City- and organizer-facing policy briefs, including just cause,
  rent stabilization, tenant and community opportunity to purchase, rental
  registries, and eviction-record and tenant-screening protections.
